name: Limostatin

lead: Limostatin is a signalling peptide discovered in fruit flies. When food is scarce, gut endocrine cells release it and it tells insulin-producing cells to release less insulin; metabolism-minded readers cite it as a model for how fasting signals fat handling and leanness.

It was the first well-characterised example of a fasting-induced hormone that opposes insulin. In the original 2015 study, flies lacking limostatin developed high insulin, low blood sugar and extra body fat. The published work is confined to flies and laboratory models.

paras: There is no product or routine; it appears in fat-loss and metabolism peptide lists because of its insulin-lowering role.
No human safety or efficacy data have been published, and effects in people have not been tested.

angle.text: Limostatin is a fruit-fly hormone that suppresses insulin during fasting, and metabolism-minded readers cite it as a model for how fasting changes fat storage signals and could lead to a leaner body. It has been studied only in insects.

lead: Limostatin (Lst) is a peptide hormone first identified in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. It is released from gut-associated endocrine cells when nutrients are scarce and suppresses the production and secretion of insulin-like peptides, which made it the first well-characterised example of a "decretin", a fasting-induced hormone that opposes insulin.[1][2]

Its connection to appearance runs through body composition. Insulin is a main driver of fat storage, and flies lacking the limostatin gene showed high insulin levels, low blood sugar and extra body fat in the original 2015 study.[1] People who follow metabolism and fat-loss peptide research therefore sometimes list it among molecules that lower insulin output; the chain is lower insulin signalling, less fat storage, leaner body composition. That chain has been examined only in insects and cells.

The mammalian counterpart is neuromedin U (NMU), a neuropeptide that the 2015 study reported suppresses insulin secretion from human islets.[1][3] No human trial of limostatin or an NMU-based product for appearance has been reported, and no source reviewed documents its use for body-composition goals in people.[1][4]
infobox: Suppresses insulin secretion under nutrient restriction
CG9918, a Drosophila ortholog of neuromedin U receptors[1]

paras: Researchers identified limostatin through genetic screens in Drosophila and reported it in 2015 as a hormone induced by nutrient restriction in gut-associated endocrine cells. Loss of the limostatin gene led to hyperinsulinemia, hypoglycemia and excess adiposity in the flies, and a conserved 15-residue peptide encoded by the gene suppressed insulin secretion.[1] The name refers to Limos, the Greek goddess of starvation.[2]

Reviews of insect lipid metabolism and of fly gut-brain signalling place limostatin among the peptide hormones that coordinate fat storage and energy use between the gut, the insulin-producing cells and the fat body.[4][5]

The 2015 study opened from a concept: decretins, hormones induced by fasting that suppress insulin production and secretion, had been postulated from classical human metabolic studies but had not been identified. The authors found Drosophila Limostatin through genetic screens [1]. Seung K. Kim is among the authors listed by Wikipedia [2].

The study proposed that knockdown of CG9918, a fly ortholog of the neuromedin U receptors, in insulin-producing cells reproduced limostatin deficiency and reduced the insulin suppression produced by purified limostatin, suggesting CG9918 encodes a limostatin receptor. It reported that NMUR1 is expressed in islet beta cells, that purified NMU suppresses insulin secretion from human islets, and that a human NMU variant that co-segregates with familial early-onset obesity and hyperinsulinemia fails to suppress insulin secretion [1].

sections.h: Neuromedin U and the human connection
paras: Neuromedin U is a conserved neuropeptide first isolated from the spinal cord in 1985 and named for its ability to contract uterine muscle. Human NMU has 25 amino acids, and it acts through two receptors: NMUR1, mainly peripheral with the highest levels in the gastrointestinal tract, and NMUR2, mainly in the central nervous system [6]. Wikipedia's NMU article lists appetite, blood pressure, pain perception, bone growth and hormone release among its functions [6].

The 2024 West Nile virus study describes NMU as the mammalian ortholog of limostatin, a peptide that regulates the production and secretion of insulin from pancreatic beta cells [3]. The genetic-obesity variant reported in 2015 is the main human-genetics link between this pathway and body weight [1].

A 2024 study in Drosophila and human cell culture reported that limostatin mutants, which have elevated insulin-like peptide expression, were less susceptible to West Nile virus infection because insulin signalling upregulated JAK/STAT immune activity; the authors used fly and human cell models to study limostatin and its human ortholog [3].

A 2026 paper described limostatin as an enterokine, produced by a small group of larval midgut enteroendocrine cells, that acts systemically to inhibit expression and release of the insulin-like peptide dIlp2 and helps coordinate developmental pace when amino acids are restricted. Its secretion is triggered by reduced amino acid availability through a relay involving the fat body and insulin-producing neurons, and the authors extend the decretin concept to developmental pace control [7].

Reviews of insect lipid metabolism and of fly gut-brain signalling place limostatin among the peptide hormones that coordinate fat storage and energy use between the gut, insulin-producing cells and fat body [4][5].
No studies found. Research on limostatin is limited to Drosophila and related laboratory models, with human islet and cell-culture experiments testing its mammalian counterpart NMU.[1][3][7]

Limostatin has no consumer product. It appears in research-peptide and metabolism discussions as an insulin-lowering signal, and no source reviewed reports people using it. Its inclusion in this wiki reflects interest in peptides that influence insulin and fat storage rather than any documented use.

timeline.event: Limostatin reported as a fasting-induced decretin hormone in Drosophila.[1]
